Divine
di-VYNE
adj., v.
From Latin divinus, belonging to a god. Webster 1828 gives the adjective — pertaining to the true God; proceeding from God — and a separate verb, to foretell or to practise divination. Both are in the Authorized Version, and they must not be confused: the adjective belongs to God, the verb to the diviner.

Biblical Definition

The KJV uses divine as two distinct words. As an adjective it marks what belongs to God: Hebrews describes the tabernacle order as ordinances of divine service, and a worldly sanctuary (Hebrews 9:1); Peter says his divine power hath given unto us all things that pertain unto life and godliness (2 Peter 1:3), and, most remarkably, that believers might be partakers of the divine nature, having escaped the corruption that is in the world through lust (2 Peter 1:4). Proverbs uses it of a king’s judgment: A divine sentence is in the lips of the king (Proverbs 16:10) — an oracle, a weighty verdict. As a verb it means to practise divination, and Scripture condemns it wherever it is not merely reporting. Joseph says of his cup, wot ye not that such a man as I can certainly divine? (Genesis 44:15), speaking as an Egyptian ruler to brothers who do not know him. Ezekiel judges the false prophetesses: ye shall see no more vanity, nor divine divinations (Ezekiel 13:23), and the diviners of Jerusalem divine a lie unto thee (Ezekiel 21:29). The adjective and the verb sit a page apart and point in opposite directions — what proceeds from God, and what pretends to.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 gives DIVINE, adj., as pertaining to the true God, proceeding from Him, excellent in the highest degree; and DIVINE, v., as to foreknow, to foretell, to use or practise divination. The KJV employs both, and they are opposite in moral direction.

expand to see more

DIVINE, a. [L. divinus.] — Pertaining to the true God; as, the divine nature; divine perfections.

Proceeding from God; as, divine judgments; divine grace.

Excellent in the highest degree; extraordinary; apparently above what is human.

DIVINE, v.t. — To foreknow; to foretell; to presage. To deify. To use or practise divination.

DIVINE, n. — A minister of the gospel; a theologian — the sense in which the Westminster and Baptist assemblies were composed of divines.

Key Scripture

Genesis 44:15 — "And Joseph said unto them, What deed is this that ye have done? wot ye not that such a man as I can certainly divine?"

Proverbs 16:10 — "A divine sentence is in the lips of the king: his mouth transgresseth not in judgment."

Ezekiel 13:23 — "Therefore ye shall see no more vanity, nor divine divinations: for I will deliver my people out of your hand: and ye shall know that I am the LORD."

Hebrews 9:1 — "Then verily the first covenant had also ordinances of divine service, and a worldly sanctuary."

2 Peter 1:4 — "Whereby are given unto us exceeding great and precious promises: that by these ye might be partakers of the divine nature, having escaped the corruption that is in the world through lust."

Modern Corruption

2 Peter 1:4 is the most abused verse in this family. Partakers of the divine nature is corrupted into deification of the creature — whether in Eastern theosis pressed past its limits, in the Word of Faith teaching that believers are little gods, or in the therapeutic notion of a divine spark within.

expand to see more

Peter’s own sentence sets the limits. Believers become partakers of the divine nature by these — that is, by the exceeding great and precious promises — and the immediate content is moral: having escaped the corruption that is in the world through lust. What is imparted is holiness, a real participation in the moral likeness of God through regeneration and sanctification, not a share in His incommunicable being. God’s aseity, immutability, simplicity, and omnipotence are not distributable. The Creator-creature distinction is not abolished in glory; it is the permanent condition of the redeemed. Any reading that makes a Christian divine in essence has crossed the line Scripture will not cross, and the Word of Faith teaching that believers are gods in the same class as God is a plain heresy on this verse.

The verb runs the other way and is the age’s live temptation. Ezekiel 13 is God’s judgment on women who sewed pillows and prophesied out of their own hearts, and it ends with the promise that they shall divine divinations no more. The New Testament closes the canon and the office; there is no continuing gift by which a man may tell another the secret will of God for his life. Where modern prophetic ministries offer exactly that — a word about a marriage, a job, a move — the form of Ezekiel 13 has returned, however warm the intention. The believer’s guidance is the sufficient Scripture, the ordinary means of grace, wisdom, and the counsel of the church.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

The Greek adjective is theios, belonging to God; the Hebrew verb behind the KJV’s divine is qasam, to practise divination, or nachash, to use enchantment. The English word carries both because Latin did.

expand to see more

Greek theios (G2304) — divine, belonging to God; divine power and divine nature (2 Peter 1:3-4), divine service (Hebrews 9:1).

Hebrew qesem (H7081) — divination; behind a divine sentence is in the lips of the king (Proverbs 16:10), where the KJV uses the noun of a weighty oracle.

Hebrew nachash (H5172) — to practise enchantment, to divine; Joseph’s words in Genesis 44:15.

Hebrew qasam (H7080) — to divine; nor divine divinations (Ezekiel 13:23), a cognate accusative the KJV preserves.

The English noun divine for a theologian gives the historic title of the Westminster Assembly of Divines, and is Webster’s fifth sense.

Usage

"Ordinances of divine service (Hebrews 9:1) — the adjective; worship ordered by God rather than by taste."

"Partakers of the divine nature (2 Peter 1:4) — moral likeness through the promises, not deification of the creature."

"Nor divine divinations (Ezekiel 13:23) — the verb; the practice God ends among His people."
